title: Edith Stein (1891–1942)
hookLine: a Jewish philosopher becomes a Carmelite nun, and is murdered at Auschwitz with her sister

lines: A BOOK READ THROUGH THE NIGHT.
cards: A borrowed book, read through the night. The reader is a young philosopher, brilliant, Jewish by birth, and for years she has called herself an unbeliever.
She's staying at a friend's house, picks up the life of Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish Carmelite, and doesn't put it down. Tradition says that when she closed it at dawn, she said: this is the truth.
Edith Stein's mother kept the Jewish faith, and her daughter's choice would cost them both a great deal. Today is her road, from the lecture hall to the convent to a train going east.

teach.b: First, the thinker. She studied philosophy in Germany and worked closely with Edmund Husserl, whose way of thinking, called phenomenology, looks carefully at experience itself.

Her doctoral work was on empathy, how one person can truly feel into another's life. Second, the convert. After that night with Teresa, she asked for baptism and was received into the Catholic Church.
She taught and lectured, until the Nazi laws pushed Jewish teachers out of their posts. Third, the Carmelite. She entered Carmel in Cologne and took a new name: Teresa Benedicta of the Cross.
Benedicta, blessed. And of the cross, because she believed she was being drawn into Christ's suffering, alongside her own people's.

Saint Paul writes in Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Her sisters moved her to a Carmel in the Netherlands for safety. Fourth, the train.
In the Netherlands, she and her sister Rosa, also a Catholic convert, were arrested and sent to Auschwitz, where they were murdered.

teach.h: KILLED BECAUSE SHE WAS BORN JEWISH.
teach.b: They were killed because they were born Jewish.

The Church honors her as a saint and a martyr. Some Jewish voices have asked that her story never blur that fact, and that her death be remembered with the death of her people. Both things are true of her.

how: Catholics keep the feast of St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross in August, and she is honored as one of the patron saints of Europe; Carmelites read her writings on the cross.

games.q: you're a philosopher who has just read through the night and closed the book convinced. your mother keeps the Jewish faith. what do you do?
o: say nothing and go back to philosophy.
write a paper about the book instead.
games.why: she asked for baptism and was received into the Catholic Church, a choice that cost her and her mother a great deal.

practice: Let Edith and Rosa stand a moment in your mind, two sisters on one train, then widen it: the families on that train and the others, with names and kitchens and jokes and recipes.
You don't need to imagine the horror; just hold the people. If you pray, pray for them in your own words; if not, keep the silence for them.
